documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: AI Guidelines (archived copy)
documents.stance_why: The page says the goal is 'not to advocate for or against' AI use and gives three syllabus templates ('No AI Allowed', 'Some AI Allowed', 'Unconditional AI Allowed') for instructors to choose from, so it sets no stance itself.
documents.summary: CETL page that offers non-binding shared principles, ideas for permitted student uses, instructor uses, citation advice and three syllabus templates. It tells instructors to decide and explain their own rule.

units.why: The page frames CETL's role as informing faculty practice and policy ('seeks to inform faculty instructional practices and policies'), a statement of purpose and scope rather than a rule, so P56 with informs.
units.anchor: seeks to inform faculty instructional practices and policies

units.why: CETL says it will 'offer workshops and consultations on AI's uses and limitations for faculty'; support for faculty learning about AI is P63.
units.anchor: offer workshops and consultations on AI's uses and limitations for faculty

units.why: 'sponsor a cross-disciplinary AI faculty group' is a faculty community on AI, which P63 names; kept apart from the workshops sentence.
units.anchor: sponsor a cross-disciplinary AI faculty group

units.why: 'involved in SBoE and multi-institutional working groups' describes coalition work with other institutions, the P88 definition; not a rule, so informs.
units.anchor: We are involved in SBoE and multi-institutional working groups

units.why: The sentence says who made the shared principles and when ('created by members of the Idaho Statewide AI Alliance in January 2024'), which is P84, not the content of the principles.
units.anchor: A statement of shared principles was created by members of the Idaho Statewide AI Alliance

units.why: The principles are explicitly non-binding but users are advised to review them; an institutional framework for responsible use (P56).
units.anchor: While the principles are not hard and fast rules, it is a good idea to

units.why: The first listed principle 'People come first.' is a framework principle with no operational rule, so P56 informs.
units.anchor: People come first.

units.why: The principle calls for continuous learning about AI; P102 (stay informed about AI developments) is nearest, though this is a cultural principle, not a duty.
units.anchor: An inquiry mindset will foster a culture of continuous learning about AI.
units.fit_note: Framed as a cultural principle ('inquiry mindset') rather than a duty to follow guidance.

units.why: The principle 'Learners need equitable access to generative AI' is the P51 equity and access content.
units.anchor: Learners need equitable access to generative AI.
units.fit_note: Stated as a principle about learner access, not as an alternative or accommodation in a course.

units.why: This principle values responsive, engaged teaching but states no rule that fits a listed type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Responsive, engaged teaching matters more than ever.
units.uncovered_note: States that responsive, engaged teaching matters more than ever in the age of generative AI, without a specific rule.

units.why: The principle says privacy and copyright expectations are 'evolving rapidly'; nearest type is P52 (copyright), though it also covers privacy.
units.anchor: Expectations around privacy and copyright are evolving rapidly.
units.fit_note: Also covers privacy and notes the expectations are changing, with no stated rule.

units.why: 'Transparency is essential' is the principle behind disclosure of AI use; P24 is nearest though no submission statement is specified here.
units.anchor: Transparency is essential.
units.fit_note: Stated as a general principle, not a requirement of a statement with each submission.

units.why: The Alliance says its statement is 'a living document that will likely be modified in the future', which is P54.
units.anchor: consider their statement to be a living document that will likely be modified

units.why: The page names the risk that AI 'can absolutely prevent them from growing', a reason that AI use shortcuts skill-building (P41), not the false-mastery warning of P43.
units.anchor: can absolutely prevent them from growing

units.why: Educators 'need to be transparent about our goals' and 'the rationale we have for our decisions' on AI use; giving students the reasons behind the rule is P66.
units.anchor: we need to be transparent about our goals for our learners

units.why: Recommends a 'flipped classroom' model so practice happens in class; restructuring the course around AI is P35.
units.anchor: a shift towards a “flipped classroom” model

units.why: Case studies and project-based learning are suggested as 'venues where students are either not using AI tools, or able to integrate AI tools' under direction; assignment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: project based learning, and other high impact practices

units.why: The page says AI tools push education 'towards ways of thinking and problem solving' as the goal; a learning-goal redesign (P35) with no concrete rule.
units.anchor: towards ways of thinking and problem solving
units.fit_note: States a shift in educational goals rather than a concrete assignment or grading change.

units.why: If an instructor decides AI use jeopardizes skills, 'you may conclude that you will not allow them to use AI tools'; the instructor chooses, so P04, on the no-AI side.
units.anchor: then you may conclude that you will not allow them to use AI tools

units.why: Instructors who ban AI should 'clearly explain your decision and the reasoning'; giving reasons is P66 (the placement in the syllabus is P09 but the stress here is on the reasoning).
units.anchor: clearly explain your decision and the reasoning for your decision in your instructions and on

units.why: Suggests instructors with a ban cite 'Student Code of Conduct E-1.c', tying AI bans to the misconduct code (P36).
units.anchor: citing the Student Code of Conduct E-1.c would be useful
units.fit_note: Recommends citing the Code in the syllabus rather than classifying AI use itself.

units.why: If an instructor decides AI helps learning they choose to allow it and 'clearly explain how'; per-instructor choice is P04, on the permit side.
units.anchor: then clearly explain how you will allow your learners to use AI tools and the

units.why: Instructors who allow AI must also 'explain what you will not allow and the reasoning'; giving reasons is P66.
units.anchor: explain what you will not allow and the reasoning for your decision

units.why: 'You should communicate your policy in your syllabus, and on the instructions for your assignments' asks instructors to state AI expectations in both places: P09.
units.anchor: You should communicate your policy in your syllabus, and on the instructions for your assignments

units.why: Listed use: querying AI for 'potential research topics' and ideas for getting started; brainstorming is P15.
units.anchor: provide potential research topics, narrow the focus of research questions

units.why: Listed use: AI can give 'an outline for writing or coding' as structure for the student's own work; nearest is P15 (exploring approaches).
units.anchor: An AI text generator can provide an outline for writing or coding
units.fit_note: Outlining a structure for writing or coding, not only brainstorming ideas.

units.why: Listed use: proofreading or rewording one's own writing is allowed; this is P91.
units.anchor: One can use an AI text generator to proofread writing

units.why: Listed use: AI can create annotated bibliographies pointing to possible sources; no type covers source-finding.
units.anchor: AI text generators can create annotated bibliographies
units.uncovered_note: AI may be used to collect candidate sources by generating annotated bibliographies.

units.why: Listed use: students draft with AI and compare against a rubric to learn the standards, a self-check of knowledge (P14).
units.anchor: Learners could create a draft of a writing or coding prompt to compare it against
units.fit_note: The aim is to internalize evaluation standards by comparing a draft with a rubric.

units.why: Listed use: AI-generated analysis of themes that students compare with their own analysis; practice or self-check (P14).
units.anchor: AI text generators can provide an analysis of themes in a piece of writing, art,
units.fit_note: Students explore or compare their own analysis with an AI one.

units.why: Instructors are told it is 'perfectly acceptable not to use them', a permission about instructors' own AI use, so P59.
units.anchor: It’s perfectly acceptable not to use them
units.fit_note: Says non-use is acceptable, with no use named.

units.why: Instructors may use AI to generate learning outcomes (a listed assistance in course materials), which P59 covers.
units.anchor: Generating learning outcomes

units.why: Instructors 'will need to use your own expertise to review the generated outcomes', a review duty for AI-made materials: P48.
units.anchor: You will need to use your own expertise to review the generated outcomes
units.fit_note: Requires review but not disclosure of AI-made materials.

units.why: AI may help instructors create rubrics, a listed instructor use covered by P59.
units.anchor: Creating assignment rubrics

units.why: Instructors should refine prompts and use their own judgement when finalizing rubrics, which P48 covers (review of AI-made materials).
units.anchor: you will likely need to refine your prompts and use your own judgement
units.fit_note: Mixes prompt refinement with human final judgement.

units.why: The page says text generators have 'a deserved reputation for making up source material' yet may help find materials; the warning about errors is P31.
units.anchor: Text generators have a deserved reputation for making up source material
units.fit_note: Mixed with a suggestion that even faulty output can help.

units.why: AI can suggest learning materials to instructors even when faulty; an instructor use covered by P59.
units.anchor: They can provide mostly accurate information on learning materials that could be appropriate

units.why: AI may assist instructors outlining or revising a course; instructor use covered by P59.
units.anchor: AI text generators may assist you as you map out a new course

units.why: Instructors keep 'the final say in how your course is taught and the learning materials'; humans stay in charge of AI-assisted course design: P59.
units.anchor: You have the expertise and responsibility to have the final say
units.fit_note: States instructor responsibility over AI-assisted design rather than a permitted use.

units.why: 'It is important to be transparent when using large language model generative AI applications in your work' calls for disclosure of AI use, P24.
units.anchor: It is important to be transparent when using large language model generative AI applications in

units.why: The page notes AI chats 'are not retrievable by others', so citation is hard; this goes to citing the tool and output (P25) and is informs.
units.anchor: the “chat” in applications like ChatGPT are not retrievable by others
units.fit_note: Names the difficulty of citing a chat rather than prescribing what to include.

units.why: Directs readers to APA, Chicago and MLA recommendations for citing AI; citation conventions are P25.
units.anchor: Style guides such APA, Chicago Manual of Style, and MLA have recommendations on when to
units.fit_note: Defers to style guides without naming what a citation must include.

units.why: The page lets users choose how to reference AI use ('the key is to be transparent'); disclosure itself is P24.
units.anchor: While you may have to make your own decision on the best way to reference
units.fit_note: Leaves the citation form open.

units.why: Offers three syllabus templates (no AI, some AI, unconditional AI allowed), i.e. named tiers of AI use: P05.
units.anchor: three examples of language you can include in your syllabus depending on your level of

units.why: 'Our goal is ... not to advocate for or against' use of AI tools; the center takes no stance and leaves the decision to instructors: P04.
units.anchor: not to advocate for or against your use or your students use of such tools
units.fit_note: The center states its own neutrality rather than assigning the decision.

units.why: 'We welcome your feedback and collaboration' invites input on the guidance, P54.
units.anchor: We welcome your feedback and collaboration on this issue.

units.why: Lists the 'AI detection feature through Turnitin for Canvas Assignments' as a software resource, a detector available for finding misuse: P40.
units.anchor: AI detection feature through Turnitin for Canvas Assignments
units.fit_note: Listed only as a resource, with no rule on when to use it.

units.why: A recorded workshop on 'Engineering Effective Prompts for AI' is offered as a resource: advice on prompting, P93.
units.anchor: Chat With Me: Engineering Effective Prompts for AI
units.fit_note: Only a workshop title, not advice itself.

units.why: The list of recorded CETL workshops on AI is faculty support to learn AI, P63.
units.anchor: Previously Recorded CETL Workshops

documents.title: Syllabus Language for AI
documents.stance_why: The article says '(please choose one or specify your own)' and gives three options, so the university sets no single rule and delegates to instructors with named tiers.
documents.summary: Three syllabus statements from the teaching center, from banned to permitted with acknowledgement, that instructors pick from. Misuse and nondisclosure are tied to the Student Code of Conduct.

units.why: The syllabus language is offered with 'please choose one or specify your own', so the instructor sets the rule: P04.
units.anchor: please choose one or specify your own

units.why: Three labelled options (prohibited, prior permission, acknowledgement) form named tiers of AI use: P05.
units.anchor: OPTION 1) AI Use Prohibited

units.why: The shared intro says 'it is important to clarify how they may or may not be used in this course'; stating expectations in the syllabus is P09.
units.anchor: it is important to clarify how they may or may not be used in this

units.why: Option 1 says use of AI tools 'is not permitted in this course', a default ban for graded work: P01.
units.anchor: is not permitted in this course

units.why: The listed tools 'ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity, Grammarly, image generators, and automated coding/writing assistants' define what the ban covers: P61 (it also names editor tools, partial P07).
units.anchor: including but not limited to ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity, Grammarly

units.why: 'Unauthorized use of AI tools is considered a form of unauthorized assistance': AI misuse classed as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: is considered a form of unauthorized assistance

units.why: The ban is justified because the course 'is intentionally designed to build foundational skills' that need 'direct engagement': P41.
units.anchor: intentionally designed to build foundational skills

units.why: Option 1's ban has an exception 'unless explicitly allowed by the instructor for a specific assignment', so assignment-level decisions: P04.
units.anchor: unless explicitly allowed by the instructor for a specific assignment

units.why: 'will be treated as a violation of academic integrity and may result in sanctions': misuse is misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: will be treated as a violation of academic integrity

units.why: Students must follow university academic honesty policies and consult the Code: P77 (existing policy).
units.anchor: Students are responsible for reviewing and adhering to all university policies regarding academic honesty

units.why: Option 2 allows AI 'only with prior instructor permission', a banned-unless-permitted default: P06.
units.anchor: only with prior instructor permission

units.why: Students must 'Email a description of your AI request to your instructor' before the assignment, ask-before-use: P10.
units.anchor: Email a description of your AI request to your instructor

units.why: 'Unless permission is explicitly granted, all assignments must be completed independently and without assistance from automated tools': default ban, P01.
units.anchor: all assignments must be completed independently and without assistance from automated tools

units.why: Under permission students 'must (1) cite any AI-generated material using a clear attribution and appropriate citation format': P24.
units.anchor: must (1) cite any AI-generated material using a clear attribution

units.why: Students must add a 2-3 sentence note on how the tool was used 'including the prompt or settings'; nearest P25 (tool, prompt).
units.anchor: include a brief (2–3 sentence) note explaining how the tool was used, including the prompt
units.fit_note: Also requires a brief note on how the tool was used, a reflection-like statement.

units.why: 'Unauthorized or undisclosed use ... will be considered a violation ... and may affect your grade': nondisclosure is the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Unauthorized or undisclosed use of AI tools will be considered a violation of academic integrity

units.why: 'This practice helps you reflect on your learning process and ensures transparency': the reason given for documenting AI use, P66.
units.anchor: ensures transparency in your academic work
units.fit_note: Gives the rationale for a disclosure rule rather than the rule.

units.why: 'If you're unsure how to document or cite AI use, please reach out or visit the University of Idaho Writing Center': human support, P72.
units.anchor: please reach out or visit the

units.why: Option 3 says AI tools 'may be used in this course if that use is properly documented and cited': permitted with disclosure, P02.
units.anchor: may be used in this course if that use is properly documented and cited

documents.title: Student Conduct
documents.stance_why: AI is listed as 'prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools' only where an instructor prohibits it, and students are told 'each instructor may have different limits', so the page defers the AI rule to instructors.
documents.summary: Dean of Students conduct page. AI appears only as a form of prohibited assistance in the definition of academic dishonesty and in a reminder that instructors set their own limits.

units.why: The Code lists 'reliance on prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools' as prohibited behavior under academic dishonesty: unauthorized AI is misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: reliance on prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools

units.why: 'individual instructors may establish additional academic integrity expectations for their courses' leaves course rules to instructors; AI is named in a later line: P04.
units.anchor: individual instructors may establish additional academic integrity expectations for their courses
units.fit_note: Stated for academic integrity expectations generally, not AI specifically.

units.why: Students are told to review instructor expectations in syllabi 'carefully': P78.
units.anchor: be sure to review them carefully
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific.

units.why: 'each instructor may have different limits or expectations of use' of AI: one course's AI rule does not carry over: P11.
units.anchor: each instructor may have different limits or expectations of use

units.why: 'Read your course syllabus carefully!' tells students to find each course's AI rules: P78.
units.anchor: Read your course syllabus carefully!

notes: Option 3 of the syllabus article repeats the Option 2 citation and misconduct sentences exactly; coded once under Option 2. Conduct page: general academic-dishonesty sentences that do not mention AI (e.g. 'unauthorized materials, sources or assistance', instructor penalties) were not coded. The CETL page is an archived copy (Wayback 2025).
